Queens enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a 21-13 overall record. The Royals finished the 2025-26 regular season 18-13 and 13-5 in ASUN play, earned the No. 3 seed in the league tournament, then beat West Georgia in the quarterfinals and Central Arkansas 98-93 in overtime in the ASUN title game to improve to 21-13 overall. Queens’ first NCAA Tournament game as a Division I member is against Purdue on Friday, March 20, 2026. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/3/3/mens-basketball-three-royals-land-asun-postseason-honors-ahead-of-conference-tournament.aspx))

Offensively, Queens is built like a modern spread attack: high-volume three-point shooting, fast scoring runs, and multiple ballhandlers rather than one heliocentric creator. In mid-February, the program’s own game notes listed Queens at 84.2 points per game, first in the ASUN and 33rd nationally, plus 10.3 made threes per game, 30th nationally. Those numbers are not cosmetic; they show up in game film and box scores. Against Bellarmine on January 3, Queens hit a school-record 24 threes in a 98-76 win, with Chris Ashby scoring 34 points and going 11-of-20 from deep. Against Eastern Kentucky on January 1, the Royals turned a 24-23 edge into separation by making four straight shots, then later answered a 67-63 deficit with an 8-0 run led by freshman guard Jordan Watford. Against North Alabama on January 21, head coach Grant Leonard explicitly said his staff anticipated UNA would try to run Queens off the three-point line, and the Royals countered by leaning into interior scoring and balanced offense in an 87-62 win. That tells you this is not just random shotmaking; Queens game-plans counters depending on how opponents guard Ashby and the arc. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/2/13/mens-basketball-queens-hosts-reigning-asun-tournament-champions-from-lipscomb.aspx))

Specific offensive personnel clarifies the scheme. Ashby is the movement shooter and spacing warper; he leads the team with 109 made threes and exploded for 10 made threes in the ASUN final. Nasir Mann is the senior connector who can rebound and initiate; in the Bellarmine blowout he posted eight points, 10 rebounds, and a career-high eight assists, a strong indicator Queens uses him as a secondary creator and hit-ahead passer. Yoav Berman is the half-court stabilizer, averaging 13.0 points, 3.7 rebounds, and 3.7 assists, and raising that to 14.4 points and 4.4 assists in ASUN play. Watford, a freshman, adds downhill creation and pick-and-roll juice, averaging 11.5 points and 3.8 assists; he scored a career-high 26 against a “strong defense” in the game preceding February 13. Avantae Parker is the frontcourt finisher and rim runner, averaging 11.6 points, 5.1 rebounds, and 1.3 blocks, and producing a 17-point, 12-rebound double-double at North Florida. The common pattern is five-out or four-out spacing around Parker dives, drive-and-kick creation from Berman/Watford/Mann, and heavy shot volume from Ashby and Carson Schwieger on the perimeter. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/local/charlotte/2026/03/16/ncaa-tournament-queens-royals))

Defensively, Queens is better described as opportunistic than suffocating. The Royals want enough stops to fuel offense, not a 58-possession grind. Their February 13 notes said opponents were averaging 78.3 points per game in league play, only sixth-best scoring defense in the ASUN, while Queens paired that with the league’s best offense. But there are targeted examples of real defensive bite. Leonard called the second half against Bellarmine “by far the best second-half defense we’ve played this season” after the Royals won 98-76. In the ASUN opener against Eastern Kentucky, Queens used what the staff itself called a “gritty second-half defensive performance” to close out a 91-89 win. In the ASUN quarterfinal against West Georgia, Queens held the Wolves to 63 points, 34 percent shooting, and 13 percent from three while forcing 14 turnovers. The philosophy appears to be pressure the ball enough to create transition offense, switch or scramble around the arc with rangy guards, and trust Parker’s shot blocking behind the play. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/2/13/mens-basketball-queens-hosts-reigning-asun-tournament-champions-from-lipscomb.aspx))

Leonard’s coaching philosophy is visible in documented in-game adjustments. The clearest example came January 21 versus North Alabama. Leonard said his staff spent time on the possibility that UNA would run Queens off the three-point line, “which they did,” and Queens responded by producing an 87-62 win behind Parker’s 18 points, nine rebounds, and three blocks and five Royals in double figures. That is a concrete adjustment from perimeter-first to paint-and-balance offense. Another example came January 1 versus Eastern Kentucky: after surrendering a 14-2 run to end the first half, Queens trailed 67-63 with 10:41 left, then answered with an 8-0 burst keyed by Watford to retake control. In the ASUN quarterfinal against West Georgia, Queens built its margin with consecutive 12-2 runs, then called timeout when the Wolves cut the lead with a 10-0 spurt, successfully stopping the slide and finishing the game. Even the ASUN title game showed adjustment capacity: Queens trailed 34-30 at halftime, then scored 52 second-half points on 51.5 percent shooting and 50 percent from three before winning overtime 98-93. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/1/21/mens-basketball-five-royals-reach-double-figures-as-queens-remains-perfect-in-asun-play.aspx?utm_source=openai))

Clutch and late-game execution is one of the strongest arguments for Queens as a dangerous 15-seed. On January 1, Queens beat Eastern Kentucky 91-89 by going 4-for-4 at the foul line in the final minute after EKU hit late threes. On February 28, Queens lost 84-79 at Central Arkansas, but the box score shows the Royals cut the margin to three on Chris Ashby’s three-pointer with five seconds left after repeated free-throw pressure situations; even in defeat, that game showed composure and shotmaking under duress. The signature clutch performance was March 8 in the ASUN final: down 34-30 at halftime against No. 1 seed Central Arkansas, Queens won the second half 52-47, then the overtime period 16-11 to win 98-93. Nine lead changes and four ties underline that this was a possession-game they finished. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/1/1/mens-basketball-gritty-second-half-defensive-effort-sends-queens-past-eastern-kentucky-in-asun-opener.aspx))

Key players start with Nasir Mann, the team scoring leader at 13.4 points per game and 457 total points, with all 34 starts. He is not just a scorer; his 17-point, 12-rebound double-double against West Georgia in the ASUN quarterfinals and near triple-double against Bellarmine show his all-around value. Berman is probably the steadiest half-court offensive piece, with 13.0 points and 3.7 assists per game overall, 14.4 and 4.4 in league play, plus a career-high 24 points against Eastern Kentucky in conference action. Parker is the interior force: 11.6 points, 5.1 rebounds, 1.3 blocks, career-high 22 points in a win over Lipscomb, 18 and 9 with 3 blocks against North Alabama, and 17 and 12 at North Florida. Watford gives them a freshman change-up creator with 11.5 points and 3.8 assists per game and the 26-point breakout noted in mid-February. Ashby is the swing piece for tournament upset math: 109 made threes on the season, 34 points with 11 threes versus Bellarmine, and 10 made threes in the ASUN championship. If he has a nuclear shooting night, Queens can score with almost anyone for 40 minutes. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/local/charlotte/2026/03/16/ncaa-tournament-queens-royals))

The notable wins reveal their ceiling. Beating Bellarmine 98-76 on January 3 showed just how devastating Queens is when the three-point volume snowballs; 24 made threes and Ashby’s 34-point outburst turned the game into a rout. The 91-89 win over Eastern Kentucky on January 1 revealed late-game poise and the ability to survive a fast, shotmaking-heavy contest. The 87-62 win over North Alabama on January 21 showed adaptability when the three-point line was taken away. The 98-93 overtime win over Central Arkansas on March 8 showed championship-level composure against the league’s No. 1 seed. On the loss side, the 100-90 home defeat to Central Arkansas on January 28 exposed their defensive limitations in a high-possession game. The 95-87 loss to Austin Peay on February 11, referenced in pregame notes as a matchup where AP’s Collin Parker scored 39, underscored the issue Queens can have containing high-end individual scorers. The 84-79 regular-season-finale loss at Central Arkansas on February 28 showed they can rally, but also that physical top-end teams can pressure them into playing from behind. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/1/3/mens-basketball-historic-afternoon-sends-queens-past-bellarmine-ashby-ties-school-record-for-threes-in-a-single-game.aspx))

As for NCAA Tournament history, head coach Grant Leonard has no prior NCAA Tournament history as a Division I head coach before 2026. Queens moved to Division I in 2022, 2025-26 was the first season the school was eligible for full NCAA postseason play, and the March 2026 berth is the program’s first NCAA Tournament appearance in the Division I era. So Leonard’s NCAA Tournament résumé entering this event is: 2026, qualified; first appearance; no prior rounds reached at the Division I level. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/local/charlotte/2026/03/16/ncaa-tournament-queens-royals))

Bottom line: Queens is a real upset threat because its offensive identity is specific and repeatable, not flimsy. The Royals spread the floor, bomb threes, run in waves, and have multiple creators who can punish overhelp. Their weakness is equally clear: they are not an elite full-season defense, and physical opponents with shot creators have scored big on them. But teams seeded on the top two lines still hate playing opponents that can make 15-plus threes, erase deficits quickly, and trust three or four different guards late. Queens checks all of those boxes with named evidence from January through March.

Queens enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as one of the more analytically interesting automatic qualifiers in the field: a team with a legitimately strong offense, a highly vulnerable defense, and a profile that looks much more volatile than its win-loss record alone suggests. The Royals finished 21-13 overall and 13-5 in ASUN play, then won the ASUN Tournament to secure the bid. Their résumé-based and predictive rankings converge in the same general band: NCAA NET No. 189, KenPom No. 183, ESPN BPI No. 193, and Bart Torvik/T-Rank No. 200 on the March 15-17, 2026 data snapshots that were publicly accessible. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2511/queens-university-royals?utm_source=openai))

From a pure efficiency standpoint, Queens is offense-first to an extreme degree. Sports-Reference lists the Royals with a 118.7 offensive rating, 39th nationally, and a 116.0 defensive rating, 349th nationally. In other words, this is a top-40 offense paired with a bottom-20 defense. Their raw scoring profile supports that split: 84.9 points per game, 22nd in Division I, but 82.9 points allowed per game, 353rd nationally. Their SRS is -3.12 with a strength of schedule of -4.78, which places the schedule outside the national top tier and helps explain why a 21-win team still sat around 190 in the major rating systems. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/queens-nc/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

The shooting and possession data paint a very clear picture of how Queens plays. ESPN’s team totals show 566 made field goals on 2,046 attempts, plus 346 made threes on 962 attempts. That works out to an effective field-goal rate of 61.1%, an excellent mark by any standard. Their three-point attempt rate is 47.0%, meaning nearly half of all field-goal attempts come from behind the arc. Their free-throw rate is 0.374, and the team shot 73.9% at the foul line. Queens also averaged just 10.7 turnovers per game; using the accessible season totals, that translates to an estimated turnover rate around 11.4%, which is very low. They grabbed 348 offensive rebounds against 801 defensive rebounds allowed to opponents, an estimated offensive rebounding rate of 30.3%. Taken together, this is a modern spacing-and-shotmaking offense: lots of threes, strong efficiency, decent offensive rebounding, and relatively clean ball security. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2511/sort/offensiveRebounds))

Personnel-level shooting reinforces the same conclusion. Chris Ashby made 109 threes at 37.5%; Carson Schwieger hit 41.1%; Maban Jabriel shot 43.9%; Avantae Parker shot 41.7% while finishing 68.5% overall from the field; and Yoav Berman shot 32.7% from deep while leading the team in scoring at 13.4 points per game. Jordan Watford added 12.6 points and 3.7 assists per game, while Nasir Mann contributed 11.9 points on 59.9% shooting. This is not a one-gun offense; it is a multi-option attack with both rim finishing and perimeter volume. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2511/sort/offensiveRebounds))

What keeps Queens from grading as a dangerous sleeper in the predictive systems is the defense. The Royals’ 116.0 defensive rating and 82.9 points allowed per game indicate a group that has real trouble containing dribble penetration, defending in space, and surviving step-up competition. The Quad 1 results are especially revealing: they went 0-5 in such games, losing at Villanova 94-74, at Virginia 94-69, at Wake Forest 111-73, at Arkansas 108-80, and at Auburn 106-65. Even accounting for opponent quality and hostile road environments, the recurring pattern is that high-major athletes and efficient offenses were able to score into the 90s or 100s against Queens with regularity. ([bballnet.com](https://bballnet.com/teams/queens-nc))

Recent form is better than the overall national rating suggests, which is one reason they were able to win the ASUN Tournament. ESPN’s schedule/results page shows Queens finishing the regular season and conference tournament on a strong run, including wins over North Alabama, West Georgia, Austin Peay, and Central Arkansas, with only a narrow late loss at Central Arkansas interrupting the stretch. Their record was 20-13 at the end of the regular season NET snapshot and 21-13 after the ASUN title run, so the last several games were mostly positive. That suggests the trend line over the final 10 games was directionally upward, even if the publicly accessible sources did not expose a clean game-by-game adjusted efficiency table for the last 10 specifically. The practical takeaway is that Queens was playing winning basketball in March, but still against a league context that the national metrics viewed as modest. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2511/queens-university-royals?utm_source=openai))

The biggest divergence between the numbers and casual perception is this: Queens may look like a typical small-conference Cinderella because of the automatic bid and mid-major label, but analytically they are not built like a slow, defense-and-execution upset team. They are built like a high-variance shotmaking team. Conventional wisdom might assume a 21-win ASUN champion is disciplined and defense-driven; the data says the opposite. Queens is explosive offensively, unusually three-heavy, and extremely fragile defensively. They can absolutely put stress on a favorite if the threes fall, because a top-40 offense with a 47% three-point attempt rate can create a short-window avalanche. But the same profile also creates blowout risk, because if the opponent wins the athletic matchup and forces them to defend for long stretches, the Royals do not have the defensive floor that more dangerous 13- or 14-seed types usually possess. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/queens-nc/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

On balance, the statistical profile is straightforward: Queens is a below-average at-large caliber team by national rankings, with a strong offense, weak defense, moderate schedule strength, heavy perimeter reliance, and improving late-season momentum. If you are forecasting tournament behavior rather than résumé quality, the Royals project as a classic volatility team: live to score 80-plus and scare someone for 30 minutes, but also vulnerable to allowing 90 if the matchup turns against them. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/_/id/2511/queens-university-royals?utm_source=openai))
matchup-analyst:
Queens enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a 21-13 team, the ASUN tournament champion, and a profile built almost entirely around offense-first shotmaking. Their own athletic-department notes list them at 84.2 points per game, No. 33 nationally in scoring, No. 75 in KenPom adjusted offensive efficiency, and 10.3 made threes per game, which ranked No. 30 nationally at the time of the February 13 update. In ASUN play, Queens averaged 86.8 points per game and led the league in scoring offense. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/2/13/mens-basketball-queens-hosts-reigning-asun-tournament-champions-from-lipscomb.aspx))

The first thing to understand tactically is that Queens wants the game spaced, flowing, and perimeter-oriented. Chris Ashby is the signature weapon: he led the team with 109 made threes, or 3.21 per game, and exploded for 10 made threes in the ASUN title game against Central Arkansas. Against Bellarmine on January 3, Queens made a school-record 24 threes in a 98-76 win, with Ashby scoring 34 points and hitting 11-of-20 from deep. That is not a random outlier; it is the cleanest example of how dangerous their offense becomes when help defenders collapse late or zone defenders lose shooter-to-shooter communication. ([axios.com](https://www.axios.com/local/charlotte/2026/03/16/ncaa-tournament-queens-royals))

Because of that identity, the specific tactics that disrupt Queens are the ones that take away first-side catch-and-shoot rhythm and force them to play through contact before the shot. Auburn provided the clearest example on December 30, winning 106-65 while pressuring the perimeter so effectively that Queens shot just 2-for-15 from three, their lowest single-game mark since 2019. Auburn also forced 11 first-half turnovers that became 17 points and used a 15-0 run triggered by five Queens turnovers in one stretch. Winthrop showed a similar blueprint in the opener: Queens went only 6-for-30 from three, committed 17 turnovers, and allowed 15 points off those miscues in an 81-74 loss. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2025/12/30/mens-basketball-queens-falls-at-auburn-in-final-non-conference-tune-up.aspx))

So if you are asking what style of defense bothers Queens, the answer is not generic “good defense”; it is ball pressure that distorts their spacing before the shot ever goes up. Their December team notes listed Queens at 12.7 turnovers per game with a negative turnover margin of minus-2.7, while opponents were generating 7.3 steals per game against them through the first seven contests. That matters because Queens does have playmaking wings, but their offensive ecosystem still depends heavily on timely reversals and kick-out creation. When those entries are delayed, their efficiency can collapse quickly. ([storage.googleapis.com](https://storage.googleapis.com/virginiasports-com/2025/11/Virginia.pdf))

On press vulnerability specifically, the strongest available evidence says Queens can be bothered by sustained pressure. Auburn’s perimeter pressure produced the 2-for-15 three-point night and the turnover avalanche noted above. Winthrop also converted Queens’ 17 turnovers into 15 points. Those are named-game examples of pressure disrupting their offensive structure. I did not find a public 2026 game source explicitly charting Queens versus a full-court press possession-by-possession, so the safest conclusion is that pressure has hurt them demonstrably, but the available public evidence is stronger on turnover pressure than on a formally logged press metric. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2025/12/30/mens-basketball-queens-falls-at-auburn-in-final-non-conference-tune-up.aspx))

On zone vulnerability, the public 2026 sources are thinner. What is clear is that Queens has enough shooting to punish passive zone coverage when the ball moves cleanly: the Bellarmine game and the Central Arkansas title-game shootout are the best evidence of that. However, strong defenses that shrink space and contest the arc have held them down, as Auburn did. I did not find a reliable public source explicitly identifying which opponents played zone on specific possessions, so I cannot honestly assign a zone-usage percentage. The evidence-based takeaway is narrower: a soft zone is dangerous against Queens because Ashby and the surrounding wings can bury it, but an active, extended zone with hard contests and rebounding support is more viable because Queens is not overwhelmingly big on the glass. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/1/3/mens-basketball-historic-afternoon-sends-queens-past-bellarmine-ashby-ties-school-record-for-threes-in-a-single-game.aspx))

Preferred pace: Queens wants games played faster and more open than a typical half-court grinder. Their 2025-26 notes and media capsule repeatedly describe them as one of the nation’s highest-scoring mid-major offenses, and the offense is built to create volume threes and multi-player double-figure scoring nights. Queens had 15 games this season with five players in double figures, which is a strong indicator of pace plus spread-touch distribution rather than one-star heliocentrism. To force the opposite, make them execute long half-court possessions, top-lock Ashby off pindowns and flare actions, switch size onto Berman and Mann, and attack the offensive glass selectively enough to send the game into a more physical half-court script. Auburn and Winthrop both succeeded by disrupting rhythm, not by running with them. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/2/13/mens-basketball-queens-hosts-reigning-asun-tournament-champions-from-lipscomb.aspx))

Personnel-wise, Queens is skilled on the wing but not imposing by high-major NCAA Tournament standards. Their key pieces are Chris Ashby (6-2), Jordan Watford (6-5), Nasir Mann (6-5), Yoav Berman (6-6), Avantae Parker (6-9), and reserve big Gus Larson (6-10). That means they have good functional size from the 2 through the 4, but their smallest high-usage creator is Ashby at 6-2, and their frontcourt lacks the overwhelming bulk you see from elite power-conference teams. Positional mismatch map: at point/lead-guard, bigger on-ball defenders can crowd Ashby and force him into tougher creation windows; on the wings, Watford, Mann, and Berman all have usable size, so the edge there comes more from burst and physical strength than height; at the 4/5, Parker at 6-9 and Larson at 6-10 can be challenged by teams with true rim-protecting size and vertical athletes, especially on defensive rebounds and second-chance sequences. Winthrop’s 16 offensive rebounds and 20 second-chance points are the cleanest public example of Queens getting physically stressed near the rim. ([arkansasrazorbacks.com](https://arkansasrazorbacks.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Queens-Notes-vs-Arkansas.pdf))

Offensively, Queens leans more team offense than pure isolation. The evidence: Berman averaged 3.7 assists per game and 4.4 in ASUN play; Watford averaged 3.7 assists and posted single-game highs of nine assists versus Gardner-Webb and seven at Wake Forest; Queens averaged 16.0 assists per game through the first seven games and had 15 games with five players scoring in double figures. Those markers all point toward a shared-creation offense rather than one dominated by isolation volume. I did not find a trustworthy public source with exact Synergy-style isolation frequency percentages for the full 2025-26 season, so I cannot supply a defensible iso-possession percentage without inventing it. The best evidence-based description is that Queens is assist-supported, spacing-heavy, and shotmaking-driven rather than iso-heavy. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/3/3/mens-basketball-three-royals-land-asun-postseason-honors-ahead-of-conference-tournament.aspx))

The same limitation applies to exact transition offense and defense frequency percentages. Public sources available here do not provide a team-level transition-frequency table. What they do show is indirect evidence: Queens scores in bunches, leads the ASUN in scoring offense, and can turn defense into offense according to its own game notes, but also gives up big scoring totals when the game becomes loose, allowing 78.8 points per game in ASUN play and, over one late-season three-game stretch, 80.3 second-half points allowed on 46% shooting across those games. Through seven early games, opponents were scoring 83.7 points per game against Queens. That supports a practical scouting read: Queens is comfortable in an up-and-down game, but its defense is vulnerable enough that opponents should not be afraid of pace if they can win the turnover and matchup battle. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/2/27/mens-basketball-queens-and-central-arkansas-collide-in-regular-season-finale-with-momentum-on-the-line.aspx))

On coaching adaptability, Grant Leonard’s staff does show evidence of in-game adjustment. The best public example is late February, when Queens had trailed at halftime in two of three games but then scored 52.3 second-half points on 62% shooting over that stretch. Against Auburn, the Royals were much cleaner after halftime, committing only three turnovers in the second half after 11 in the first. Those are meaningful signs of halftime adjustment. I cannot honestly evaluate “mid-series” adaptability because college teams are not playing playoff series, but the available evidence suggests Leonard’s staff can improve offensive function after a poor first half. ([queensathletics.com](https://queensathletics.com/news/2026/2/27/mens-basketball-queens-and-central-arkansas-collide-in-regular-season-finale-with-momentum-on-the-line.aspx))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Queens you must 1) run Ashby off the line with top-locks and hard chase contests; 2) pressure the ball early in the clock, because Auburn and Winthrop showed their offense can bog down into turnovers; 3) make the game more physical at the rim, where Winthrop’s 16 offensive boards and 20 second-chance points exposed them; 4) force them into a half-court possession count where they have to score over set size instead of flowing into drive-kick threes; 5) attack their defense without fear, because their season profile is much stronger offensively than defensively; and 6) punish slow starts, because Queens has trailed at halftime in multiple recent games and relies on second-half recoveries. If you let Queens play with clean spacing and rhythm, Ashby, Berman, Mann, Watford, and Parker can spread 80-plus points across the lineup. If you turn the game into a pressure-and-physicality contest, the public evidence says they become beatable.
